title: How Late Payments Became A Permanent Problem
text:
How Late Payments Became A Permanent Problem

Andrew Batson, Xiaoxi Zhang

Gavekal Dragonomics | 14 Oct 2026

Why is it so hard for China’s big companies to pay their bills on time? Small and private-sector businesses have complained for years that they are rarely paid promptly by their customers, particularly state-owned enterprises and government departments. The arrears issue has been so severe for so long that it has become a potent symbol of the quality of China’s business environment for private firms, one that gets top-level government attention. Yet it seems to defy easy solution. The government has recently rolled out a new batch of measures promising tighter scrutiny and tougher enforcement, following national rules in 2025 that set higher standards—which themselves updated an earlier set of rules from 2020.These repeated efforts at least display a consistent intention, which comes from the top. In a speech to private entrepreneurs in February 2025, top leader Xi Jinping personally pledged that the government would resolve the problem of arrears. “Laws and regulations should be improved and penalties for acts of dishonesty strengthened,” he said. “We cannot allow a situation in which new arrears are incurred while old ones are being cleared, or arrears reappear after being cleared, in an endless cycle.” Yet that is exactly what is happening: the evidence suggests the cycle of delayed payments continues and arrears are still getting worse.
